notes: monthsInDate is IDENTICAL to months and that is correct, not an oversight: Filipino nouns do not inflect for case, so a month name has one form wherever it stands. THE NUMERIC ORDER IS AMERICAN, MONTH FIRST: the Philippines writes 12/25/2026 for Christmas Day, not 25/12/2026, because the convention came with the American colonial administration and never changed; this is the one thing about Philippine dates most likely to be got wrong by a European default, and a misread Philippine date is silently wrong for the first twelve days of every month. The long form is the American one too, MMMM D, YYYY with a comma. A fully Filipino long date exists and reads ika-25 ng Disyembre 2026, using the ordinal prefix ika- and the linker ng, but it belongs to formal and literary registers; ordinary Philippine documents print the English form. Month and weekday names are all SPANISH loans respelled to Filipino orthography, and they are CAPITALISED, unlike in Spanish itself. Month abbreviations take a full stop, weekday abbreviations do not. LINGGO IS BOTH SUNDAY AND 'WEEK' — isang linggo is one week, araw ng Linggo is Sunday — so the same string does two jobs and only context separates them. The weekdays array above is SUNDAY-FIRST because the formatter wants it that way, and Sunday-first is also the Philippine calendar convention: printed Philippine calendars begin the week on Sunday, following the American and Catholic pattern, unlike the Monday-first European one. Note that date/weekday.txt in the pack is Monday-first, which is how a Filipino lists the working week. Time is written in 12-hour form with AM and PM, and spoken with the Spanish hour words — alas-dos ng hapon for two in the afternoon, ala-una for one o'clock — so the spoken and written systems differ. The decimal separator is a full stop and the thousands separator a comma (1,234.56). Currency is the Philippine peso, symbol PHP, written BEFORE the amount with no space.
